1339.t: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *der-drew-om with dissimilation, reduplicated from *dóru (“tree”), but this type of reduplication is highly atypical, so the formation must be regarded as uncertain.

1371.t: Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *dʰǵʰúHs (“fish”), but the initial ἰ- (i-) is unetymological and problematic. Compare Old Armenian ձուկն (jukn) and Lithuanian žuvi̇̀s.

1381.t: From Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁- (“to cut off, separate, free”) (which Beekes reconstructs as *lh₁u-).

1375.t: From γνω- (gnō-), the root of γιγνώσκω (gĭgnṓskō, “to know”) + -μη (-mē).

1377.t: From Old Median *ganǰam (“treasure”) spread by the Achaemenid administration.

1310.t: Likely from a Proto-Indo-European *gʰelh₂d- (“hail; hoarfrost”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *žȇldъ (“glazed frost, sleet”), Persian ژاله (žâle, “hail”).

1392.t: From τρέφω (tréphō, “to maintain, support”) + -η (-ē, action noun suffix).

1367.t: From earlier Ἀρταξέσσης (Artaxéssēs), assimilated to the name Ξέρξης (Xérxēs), borrowed from Old Persian 𐎠𐎼𐎫𐎧𐏁𐏂𐎠 (a-r-t-x-š-ç-a /⁠R̥taxšaçāʰ⁠/).

1318.t: From Proto-Hellenic *iherós, from Proto-Indo-European *ish₁rós. There are a number of candidate cognates with this word; these include Sanskrit इषिर (iṣirá, “strong, active”) and Oscan 𐌀𐌉𐌔𐌖𐌔𐌉𐌔 (aisusis, “sacrifices”).

1300.t: From Proto-Hellenic *gónu (“knee”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu (“knee”). Cognates include Sanskrit जानु॑ (jā́nu), Latin genu, Old Armenian ծունգք (cungkʻ), Gothic 𐌺𐌽𐌹𐌿 (kniu), and Old English cnēow (English knee).

1332.t: Borrowed from Old Median *xšaθrapāvā, which is cognate with Old Persian 𐎧𐏁𐏂𐎱𐎠𐎺𐎠 (x-š-ç-p-a-v-a /⁠xšaçapāvā⁠/); see there for more.

1376.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *gonwía, from *gónu (“knee”, whence γόνυ (gónu)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu (“id”).

1378.t: Cognate to Sanskrit ध्रणति (dhráṇati, “to sound”), Latin drēnsō, and Old English drān (English drone). Compare also θρέομαι (thréomai, “to cry aloud, shriek”).

1330.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kʷos + -ιος (-ĭos, adjective suffix). Compare the indefinite form ποιός (poiós).

1307.t: Uncertain. Traditionally derived from a Proto-Indo-European *gʰérsdʰ-o/eh₂-, with cognates including Latin hordeum, Old High German gersta, but there are phonetic difficulties with this.

1326.t: Present passive participle of οἰκέω (oikéō, “I inhabit, dwell”). The noun use is an ellipsis of οἰκουμένη γῆ (oikouménē gê, “inhabited earth”).

1386.t: Of unknown origin, with Beekes tentatively suspecting a derivation from Pre-Greek, albeit with no particular evidence.

1388.t: From σπεύδω (speúdō, “to be keen; make haste”) + -η (-ē).

1359.t: Uncertain According to Beekes, probably of Pre-Greek origin. He is sceptical of a connection with either κρίζω (krízō, “to creak”) or Cretan ἄχηρον (ákhēron, “grasshopper”).

1356.t: Traditionally analyzed as τηρός (tērós, “a guard”) + -έω (-éō, denominative verbal suffix), though Beekes considers τηρέω (tēréō) as the original formation and τηρός (tērós) as a back-formation.

1365.t: From ἁγνός (hagnós, “sacred, pure”) + -ίζω (-ízō, denominative verb suffix).

1301.t: From διαιρέω (diairéō, “take apart, cleave, divide”) + -σις (-sis), from δια- (dia-, “apart”) + αἱρέω (hairéō, “take, grasp”).

1338.t: Related to δῶρον (dôron, “gift”), albeit with a suffix -εά (-eā́) of seemingly unclear form and function.

1311.t: No convincing Indo-European etymology; probably from Pre-Greek, as evidenced by the irregular alternation between /d/ and /tʰ/ in related terms, the latter in e.g. ψύθος (psúthos, “lie, untruth”), ψυθῶνες (psuthônes, “slanderers”) and the Homeric aorist…

1315.t: From Proto-Indo-European *sm̥-, zero-grade of *sem- (“one”). The second part is obscure, but the word may be some syncope of *ἁ-πακυς, from Proto-Indo-European *sm̥-pn̥kʷu- (“(lit.) all-one”).

1329.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pləks, probably from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”), sharing cognates with several Germanic languages through Proto-Germanic *flaką (“something flat”), *flakaz (“flat”); more at English flake.

1324.t: Uncertain. Has been connected with Ancient Greek κάλαθος (kálathos) and Latin colus, although Beekes rejects these connections.

1380.t: Possibly evolved from an original sense of “weak, flaccid”, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱremh₂- (“to hang”).

1325.t: From Proto-Indo-European *keh₂po-s (“land, garden”), which seems to be from *kap- (“to seize”) (though Beekes is skeptical of this relation and tentatively separates the two).

1372.t: From Proto-Hellenic *orút͏̌t͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewk- (“to dig up, grub”). Cognate with Latin runcō.

1350.t: Syncopic form of *πιπεράσκω (*pĭperā́skō); from *πιπεράω (*pĭperắō, reduplication of περάω (perắō, “to export for sale”)) + -σκω (-skō).

1345.t: From μετα- (meta-, “concerning change of”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).

1331.t: This verb is a secondary formation and it goes back to older *πτω-έω (*ptō-éō) (compare πτώξ (ptṓx, “hare”)); πτοιέω (ptoiéō) and other forms are derived from it by metrical lengthening.

1353.t: A zero-grade nominal form from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃- (“to drink”), though the exact derivation is unclear.
